utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the pages of the transcript as listed in document Exhibit 2 D92 that I have given to you, it appears that in court two 3 specific terms were used during the trial, "identification" and 4 "recognition". Can you tell the Court what these terms mean in 5 psychological and forensic literature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Recognition" is a very broad term that is used for any 7 situation in which stimulus is shown to a person, in which a 8 person has to express whether he or she has seen that stimulus 9 before. So that could be a face, a person, a book or words, a 10 picture, anything. In principle, all identification procedures 11 that are used in court proceedings or in police investigation 12 would fall under that broad definition. I have noticed in the pages from the records that 14 I have seen that this Court has adopted a slightly different 15 meaning of the word in which it has distinguished between 16 "identification", which is a word that is normally not used in 17 psychological theory, and "recognition", where recognition has 18 been reserved for those witnesses who know the accused before 19 the war and who have later identified him; whereas 20 "identification" has been used by this Court to indicate 21 subjects, witnesses rather, who did not know the accused before 22 the war, and who have identified him by the means of a 23 photospread. In order not to confuse matters, I have suggested in 25 my letter that I follow this terminology, that I will use 26 "recognition" for the recognition of a person that was known 27 before the war to the witnesses and "identification" by those 28 recognitions by witnesses who did not know the accused before the crime. 2 Q. Thank you. If the term "identification" was used in Court in connection with witnesses who did not know Mr. Tadic before the war and who identified him with the use of a photospread, would such identification always prove that the accused committed the crime with which he is charged? 7 A. No, definitely not. Maybe it is, if I may, it would be good to explain the logic of an identification test ---- 9 Q. If you would, please. 10 A. --- and what it purports to do. A proper identification test usually has the objective to place the accused at the scene of the crime. I mean the following. If the witness has never seen the accused before the moment of the crime and possibly at the scene of the crime, depending on whether the accused was there or not, then a later identification that would follow all the rules for identification would logically place the accused at the scene of the crime, because how can a person recognise, identify, someone if he or she has never seen that person? If there is only one occasion in which he or she can have seen that person, then, logically, it is confirmed that that person was present at that particular occasion, in this case the scene of the crime. It does only that; it locates the accused at the scene of the crime. It does not say what the accused did there, whether he was guilty of any crime or not. It only positions him at the scene of the crime. So it can definitely never confirm what that person did. That is a different question. It only contributes one 1 step, locates the person at the scene of the crime. It can only 2 do that if the identification procedures were correct. There 3 are many ways in which identification procedures can be 4 incorrect and usually when you make an error in the procedure, 5 the logic -- you lose the logic that the result places the 6 accused at the scene of the crime. For instance, if there has been another encounter 8 between the witness and the accused, you cannot logically 9 conclude that since the accused was recognised, there is only 10 one explanation which is an encounter at the scene of the 11 crime. There is another explanation which is the second 12 encounter. So, as soon as you know that there was a second 13 encounter, you lose the logic of the identification test. In my letter to you and also in my published work, 15 I have discussed many problems in identification procedures that 16 I would say almost without exception reduce or either remove the 17 logic of the test. So my answer is, no, an identification test 18 will never prove what the person did. It can only prove that 19 the accused was at the scene of the crime, but that will only 20 happen if there were no flaws in the procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean, what you have just told us, that an 22 identification by an eyewitness does not always have probative 23 value?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it very much depends upon the specific conditions in which 25 the test was made. To give you one example, if the witness knew 26 the accused even before the crime, the identification does not 27 logically lead to the conclusion that because of the 28 identification we can now know that the accused was at the scene of the crime. 2 Q. Am I right ---- 3 A. If the test was highly suggestive in one way or the other, again there is another explanation for the correct identification of the accused, namely, that it was highly suggestive -- it is too easy, anybody, even those people who were not present at the scene of the crime, would find it easy to find out to whom they should point in the test. 9 Q. Am I right in thinking then that the probative value of an identification might generally be crippled by two major issues: First of all, is there any reason to believe or to take into account that the witness knew the accused from other occasions than the crime and, secondly, was the procedure of identification correct? Are these the two major issues there? 15 A. Well, I would say the logic that the identification proves the presence of the accused at the scene of a crime is crippled by those things. You may have other objectives with an identification test. For instance, simply to verify that we are still talking about the same person, the same person that these people knew so well from many years before the war, just to exclude the mistakes or so, and that still could be very useful. But that is a different thing than the logic that possibly the test places the accused at the scene of the crime. It is that logic that is crippled by the two things that you mentioned. 26 Q. Thank you. If the term "recognition" was used for witnesses who knew Mr. Tadic before the war and who recognised him in Court as the person they had known for a long time, would such recognition always prove that the accused committed the crime with which he is charged? 3 A. No. I would say if they knew him very well before the war, a recognition during the investigation only proves that they knew him very well before the war. If there is any reason to doubt that, we have now established that. But anybody who knew him very well before the war would be able to recognise him after the war. So, logically, that does not prove that their testimony about what happened during the war is true or not true. It simply has nothing to do with it logically. 11 Q. Does this mean that recognition of an accused does not always have probative value then? 13 A. Well, it proves what it proves. It proves that they know this person, and that is what they said. If that needs proof, it has probative value. If you want to prove through the recognition that their testimony about what happened during the war is true, I would say it cannot contribute anything to that, apart from the fact that, apparently, this witness has not lied about his previous acquaintance with this person. If it is worthwhile to establish that, it does it. 21 Q. Are there major problems here that might cripple the probative value as such, that is, simply, "We know him for a long time and, therefore, we are able to recognise him"? 24 A. I do not quite understand your question. I am sorry. 25 Q. Are there problems here you could label that might cripple a claim of a witness ,"I know him from before and, therefore, I am able to recognise him"? Are there procedures that might cripple or is there anything that might cripple?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in principle, these what you call "recognitions", 2 identifications by people who knew him from before the war, in 3 principle, the identifications were done here in the courtroom. 4 They are what we call "dock identifications". Of course, the 5 situation here is very simple. It is very easy to find out who 6 of the persons present in this courtroom is the suspect, is the 7 accused. So even if they lied about knowing him before the war, 8 they would find it easy to identify him now. So if you have 9 really a doubt whether it is true that they knew him before the 10 war, I would say a better test is needed than a dock 11 identification test. On the other hand, assuming that these witnesses are 13 totally honest, and there would have been a mistake, so the 14 person they described is not the person present in the courtroom 15 today, there is every reason to assume that they would now 16 correct the mistake and say, "No, that is not the person I 17 mean". They have given all opportunity. Only when you start to 18 doubt their sincerity or their honesty, you need a more critical 19 test than a dock identification. But I have in the discussions I have read not seen any 21 description about whether it is true that they lived in the same 22 village or in the same area. So I would not directly see a need 23 for a more strict test than just a kind of verification test in 24 the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it then that "identification" and "recognition" in the 26 way it has been used in this Court require two different forms 27 of testing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For those few witnesses who did not know him before the 1 war, you need a much more strict and better controlled test, 2 because the outcome may have the logical implication that now 3 the accused is placed within the camp. I would say that 4 conclusion is so important there must be no doubt about that the 5 evidence is doing that. So that is why for those who did not 6 know him and who are going to pass an identification test, a 7 very well controlled procedure is necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe such a procedure for us, just in general 9 terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say I have described it in length in various 11 publications. The surprising thing is that although you might 12 think it is easy to do, in fact, it is not at all easy to do. 13 I have published in 1988 50 rules for such tests. That is not a 14 limited list. There are more rules. Those are the 50 most 15 important ones. In principle, what you do is that you place the person 17 whom you suspect among a number of other people whom are known 18 to be innocent and are known to be unfamiliar to the witnesses, 19 who sort of fit the same general description as the suspected 20 person. Then you ask the witnesses whether they recognise the 21 one person they have described before or not. You tell them 22 that maybe that person is not in the lineup so they should not 23 guess. They should only point at someone if they recognise him 24 positively. You tell them they can only point at one person 25 because they cannot recognise two, at one person or at nobody. 26 You give them a limited time to do that because if you recognise 27 them, you recognise them in a short time, it does not help to 28 wait two and a half hours and then you may recognise them. 1 Q. What kind of testing is generally required for what has been called in this Court "recognition"? 3 A. Well, if -- it depends on, as I said, it depends on what the purpose, the objective of what the recognition is. If it is just to verify that this is the same person that the witness described, the person has known for so long, then in Court dock identification probably would suffice. If there is sincere doubt that this person, although he claims to have known the accused for a long time, in fact never had met him, then also for that purpose you need a far more critical test like the one I described to you. But if it is not at issue, if it is not in doubt whether he knew that person, you do not need to take all those precautions. You only need to verify that we are still talking about this same person so there are no mistakes. 16 Q. Professor, before I ask you about the tests that were applied in the Tadic case, let me first ask you, did you find in your review of the transcript that 52 witnesses were confronted with the accused in one way or another? 20 A. Yes, on page 3 of my letter of 10th October, if I may refer to that letter because it is more practical, I think. There is a table which lists the number of witnesses ---- 23 Q. Before you do that, Professor, may I suggest that we provide the Court with a copy of that letter that might be helpful for you to follow the explanation? (Handed) Please continue. 26 A. So on page 3 there is a little table that represents the witnesses about whom I have read parts of the records. I do not want to imply that these are all the witnesses that have been 1 presented to the Court. Those are the witnesses that I know of 2 on the basis of this package, this extract, of the Court 3 proceedings. Of these 52, 48 declared that they knew Mr. Tadic 4 long before the war and four declared that they did not know 5 him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of those 48, can you explain to the Court how many of those 7 48 did recognise Mr. Tadic or did recognise him and their 8 conditions that would be correct if the test was applied to the 9 witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends what the objective is. Out of these 48, 42 11 identified -- no, 47 identified the accused here in the 12 courtroom. If the objective of that is just to make sure there 13 is no misunderstanding, it confirmed they recognised him, it 14 confirmed, "This is the person I am talking about", that would 15 be a correct procedure for just verifying that there is no gross 16 mistake. Five additionally also looked at photographs before 18 they came to Court, but generally (and I have described that in 19 this paragraph relating to this), these photo identifications 20 were not proper photo line ups. Some of them consist of only 21 two photos. So again also these five, about these five, we know 22 that they verify that the person being accused now is the person 23 they were talking about, and about which they declared that they 24 knew him long before. Nothing else. Then there is one witness 25 who appeared in Court, but I could not find any identification 26 attempt. So we do not -- the verification was not done. I would say, in principle, with this 47 there is 28 nothing wrong as long as the logical conclusion of those identification that is drawn by either you, the Prosecution or the Court is not that those identifications now place the accused at the scene of the crime, in the camp, because they cannot logically do that. It is only established here in Court the witness still thinks that the person he is talking about is the same as the accused. 7 Q. So you did find 48 witnesses who claimed that they did know Dusko Tadic before the war, is that correct? 9 A. Yes, and maybe I should add that a proper lineup, the way I described, is impossible with people who knew him anyway, because even if they had never seen him during the war they would find it easy to identify him. So the logic, the logic of the proper identification test, would be lost anyway. So, I think the procedures that have been used here are adequate for the limited purpose, the limited objective, of simply excluding gross mistakes. 17 Q. May I try to sum this up? Did you find 84 witnesses who claimed that they knew Mr. Tadic before the war, is that correct? 19 A. Well, I would say, rather, 48. 20 Q. 48, excuse me. 21 A. Yes. 22 Q. Right. Did you find that 42 of these 48 witnesses claimed that they recognised Mr. Tadic in the dock? 24 A. Well, no, 47. You have to add the five, those five. 25 Q. I will come to that letter. 26 A. OK. 42 identified him, as far as I know, only here and not before with the help of photographs. 28 Q. Right. 1 A. Yes. 2 Q. Did you find that five of these 48 witnesses recognised Mr. Tadic by use of a photospread and also recognised him in the dock? 5 A. Yes. I should say, of course, that since they have seen photographs of him before, there is a slight logical problem here, because if, in fact, they had never seen him before the war but only on this photograph, they would also find it possible to identify him here in Court, and certainly for those five it does not really prove that they knew him before the war because they have seen his picture during the investigations. But if you want to assume that those witnesses are honest people, they would have had -- and there is a mistake, just that the wrong person is here, then of course they would have said, "No, this is not the person I have known for so long". 17 Q. Did you find that one witness who had failed to recognise Mr. Tadic in the photo test was subsequently asked to identify him in the dock? 20 A. Wait a minute. Can you repeat the question? 21 Q. Did you find that one witness who failed to recognise Mr. Tadic in the photo test was subsequently asked to identify him in the dock? 24 A. Wait a minute, you are not referring to the one in my table where it says one person, I think, because that is a person for whom there was simply no identification attempt whatsoever, as far as I know. 28 Q. Perhaps you could read to the Court in your expert opinion the sentence beginning with "The one exception"? 2 A. That is on page 3 I think. 3 Q. On page 3, a little over the middle of the page. At the end of the sentence you will see "The one exception". It is at the top of that letter. 6 A. "With the exception of one, the 40 tests revealed positive results". 8 Q. Later on down five lines down you will find at the end of line ---- 10 A. Yes. "The one exception mentioned above was a witness who participated both in the photo test and the dock identification." OK, yes, that is the witness who failed in the photo test and later she claimed that in fact she had recognised Mr. Tadic but had failed to express that. That is a problem because if one wants to stick to the rules for identification the first response, that is the final response. You do not allow witnesses to correct their responses, and definitely not after a while when they have seen and talked to other people. 19 Q. Should a subsequent dock identification then be held after such a test or failed test? 21 A. In principle not I would say. This is a person who, according to the rules, has demonstrated that she cannot easily identify the witness. In a subsequent dock identification, as I explained, it would be rather easy for her because she has seen the picture. Of the 13 pictures she has seen, if she has had the complete test, there is one person present, so it is easy for her to realise that is the person she should point at. So the answer is, no, once there is doubt whether a witness can identify the accused, once the witness has failed to do that, I would say you should reject the witness and note it as a non-recognition, non-identification. 4 Q. Would you say then that that dock identification of that witness fails diagnostic value? 6 A. The dock identification does not have the power to sort of correct what was lost during the first identification. 8 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: May I just ask a question about that one person? Is that person in your number for the photo test or is that person in the number for the dock identification or both? 11 A. It is the person -- she is in the five. 12 Q. She is in that five? 13 A. She is one of those five because she received two tests. 14 Q. She is listed as a dock identification ---- 15 A. And photo test, yes. 16 Q. --- but for someone who knew him. Is she also in the four? No, she could not have been because she knew him? 18 A. No, she knew him. 19 Q. She is in the five. 20 A. She knew him but she could not recognise him in the 13-picture photo test. So she is within those five. 22 Q. She is in the dock identification. Thank you. 23 MR. WLADIMIROFF: So where does that leave us? How many positive recognitions were there altogether of those who claimed that they knew him before the war? 26 A. So from those who knew him before the war, those 48, 46 recognised him in one way or the other. One as far as I know was not tested and one did not pass the test. 1 Q. Thank you. Again, Professor, before focusing on the ins and outs of these recognitions in details, does this mean that these 46 recognition logically corroborate the claim of these witnesses that Mr. Tadic is the person they have seen to commit the crime? 6 A. Well, logically it corroborates that that is the person they know as Mr. Tadic. They are able to indicate who Mr. Tadic is. I would say that is a necessary condition for believing that they saw, that they know who saw commit some crimes. So, if they would not have passed the test there would have been a problem with legal evidence, because if they cannot recognise him how do they know that that was the person they saw commit crimes? It is a necessary condition. They should pass the test, but once they have passed the test there is still a question about: Is it true what they say about him? They know who it is. Of course they know if they have lived in the same village. So they are not lying about knowing who he is. That is all that is proved. 19 Q. Are you saying it does not logically corroborate the claim of these witnesses that Mr. Tadic is the person they have seen to commit the crimes? 22 A. No, logically not, because others who have lived in the village and who have never seen anybody do any crimes would found it equally easy to identify him. So the easy identification by people who are from the same village or same area, just means they are from the same area, that is all. It does not mean that they saw or did not see any crimes. 28 Q. If we proceed to the other group, those who claim that they did 1 not know him before, how many people did you find out of those 2 52 witnesses according to your review?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found four in the pages that were given to me. I consider 4 these four, although the number might seem small, are extremely 5 important because if the procedures are correct then, logically, 6 that places the accused in the camp. I think that is such an 7 important element to the Court that, even although there are 8 four, I would say four is a small number compared to 52, but it 9 is not a small number. There are four witnesses who all 10 attested they have seen him in the camp, and if they can now 11 recognise him and the tests were executed in the correct manner, 12 there is no other explanation for the recognition but the fact 13 that they saw him in the camp. So those four, it is not a small 14 number. They are extremely important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, may I ask a question? You say these 16 four are very important because of placing him in the camp. If 17 you look back to the 42 some of them knew him from childhood, we 18 will assume. They say, "We saw him in the camp". Why is that 19 evidence less important than the evidence of the four, if the 20 test for the four is properly conducted? I do not follow that 21 at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not saying that evidence is less important. What I am 23 saying is if they tell you, "We saw him in the camp", and you 24 want to confirm that because you do not believe those 25 statements, then the identifications do not help you any more. 26 If you do not believe what they said about seeing him in the 27 camp, then asking them to identify him does not help you. It 28 does not add anything. If you want to believe what they said, you do not even need the identifications. 2 Q. But we are not using identification to determine whether these witnesses are truthful or not. That is quite a different matter, a matter for the Court, is it not? 5 A. Sure, but that is exactly the reason why of those 42 or 48 depending on to whom you want to refer, their identifications do not add anything to their truthfulness. 8 Q. No, but it may not be intended to. It has nothing to do with truthfulness? 10 A. Yes. 11 Q. I follow. 12 A. Whereas the four, that is a different matter. On the basis of their identification you may decide whether they are truthful or not, because if they are not truthful it will be impossible for those four to identify him, you see. So there logically it has a different meaning. 17 JUDGE STEPHEN: Thank you. 18 MR. WLADIMIROFF: So, do these identifications of those four logically place Mr. Tadic at the scene of the alleged crimes? 20 A. They have the potential to do that, depending on whether the procedures were applied correctly or not. But they have the potential to do that, yes. 23 Q. So without correct procedures they do not have that potential? 24 A. If there are really gross violations of procedures, that potential is lost. 26 Q. Am I right in thinking then that the value of these four identifications totally depends on the procedure? 28 A. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, would it be relevant to know about other photo tests 2 with persons who were interviewed by the Prosecution or other 3 investigating bodies and who have not been called by the 4 Prosecution to give evidence in court? Would it be relevant to 5 know about the other photo tests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely for various reasons. One is that on the basis 7 of these four witnesses I could not form a clear image of the 8 procedures, the exact procedures that have been used, and maybe 9 if there were more witnesses that, bit by bit, details of those 10 procedures would come out. That is one. But the more important 11 factor is that the one thing you definitely want to know is 12 whether there were witnesses who participated in the photo test 13 and who did not recognise him. Now the score, if I may say so, 14 stands four out of four. Four represented the photo test, they 15 all identified him. If one would believe that those witnesses 16 were lying about, say, their experiences and were simply 17 guessing in the test, then this result would be highly 18 unlikely. It would be 1/13th to the power of 4 which is an 19 incredibly small number. If in fact these four witnesses are 20 four out of, say, 50 for example, and the other 46 did not 21 recognise him but we are now told about them, then certainly the 22 likelihood that four out of 50 would guess correct is rather 23 high. So if we want to exclude the possibility that people were 24 simply guessing and guessed correctly, then we have to know how 25 many witnesses participated in such tests, in total and what the 26 results of all of them were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What if one of these four or all of them would have seen a 28 photo, a previous photo test with the photo of Dusko Tadic in a different setting, in another case? 2 A. That would invalidate the test because then we cannot decide what it means that they recognised him. Does it mean that they saw him in the camp because that was the only encounter? Or does it mean they remembered from the previous photo? So the logic then, the logic of the test has gone. 7 Q. Let me focus on the major problems that might cripple the outcome of your review. I take it that a photospread should not contain such suggestive details or biasing elements that you would say that such a test is not sufficient to identify a suspect, is that correct? 12 A. Yes, all details that make it very easy to guess who the suspect in that lineup is, in principle invalidates the test. The rule is, which is a very practical rule, that if you ask people who were never involved in this whole problem to indicate who they think the accused is, they should not be able to do that. If they understand from some suggestive aspect of the lineup who the accused is, then certainly it does not mean anything any more that the witnesses can do the same. It does not prove they have seen him because others who have not seen him can do it equally easy. 22 Q. Is there a test in your field of expertise that enables you to test whether the photospread is correct or not? 24 A. Yes, that is sometimes referred to as the Doob and Kirshenbaum test and I have, as well as we could, applied that test to the set of 13 pictures. 27 Q. What does the test mean? 28 A. I reported this to Mr. Tieger in my letter of March 27th. 1 Q. May I then suggest we present a copy of that letter to the Court. Can you tell us what this test means? 3 A. The test consists of presenting the 13 pictures to we call them "subjects", or you might call them naive witnesses but I would rather call them subjects because they have nothing to do with the trial, and ask them: "One of these people is accused of being a war criminal. Have you any idea who it is?" We asked 39 subjects and their choice frequency can be found in the little table on page 3 of my letter. The picture of the accused is No. 3. So what you can see is that five out of 39 selected the accused. The guessing level is three out of 39, 1/13th. So it is slightly above the guessing level, but not significantly so. I reported in my letter that there is a problem with this test which could not be mended by me easily, which is that my subjects had the Dutch nationality, whereas the witnesses definitely had not. The problem is, and this is an hypothetical problem because at that time I could not find out how big the problem was, the problem is that imagine that people from the former Republic of Yugoslavia can easily distinguish between the various ethnic groups, and imagine additionally that Mr. Tadic is the only one who clearly looks like a Serb and the others do not. Then to people from my subjects that would be not be obvious. They would not select the picture of Mr. Tadic as the only one representing a Serb. 26 Q. By your subjects you mean Dutch? 27 A. My Dutch subjects. Witnesses who look at those things and who come from the former Republic of Yugoslavia might immediately 1 recognise there is only one Serb in the lineup and say, "Ah, 2 that must be him", because the person we are talking about is a 3 Serb. I could not easily mend that because I had no people from 4 the former Republic at my disposal as subjects. I reported this 5 problem. Since then we have run experiments in Belgrade with 7 subjects -- I still call them subjects because it has nothing to 8 do with the trial as such -- with subjects who are more or less 9 representative of, say, the group of witnesses. What we have 10 found is that also these subjects found it impossible to 11 classify the pictures according to ethnic background, which 12 suggests to me that this problem, hypothetical problem, did in 13 fact not occur. Again I must say there is an exception there 14 too. I believe I must apologise to make things so complicated 15 as scientists always do, but that is my profession. I cannot 16 help it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me take a very extreme example. Imagine that we would have 19 presented 12 pictures of Japanese people to those subjects in 20 Belgrade and asked them, "Group them according to ethnic 21 background", and then mention the Yugoslav groups like Croats, 22 Macedonians and so on. They would find it extremely difficult 23 to group the Japanese faces in these categories because they 24 simply do not fit. Of course, what you have to know is that the 25 pictures that you present are of people from the former Republic 26 of Yugoslavia. So that the question to categorise them, to 27 classify them, is a meaningful question. Unfortunately, I do not know who these 12 people, these foils in the set of 13, who they are and where they came from. So if they are not Yugoslavians at all, one reason why they could not be classified according ethnic groups is that they simply do not belong to these ethnic groups. That is a question I have to leave open. I do not know who they are and there is no easy way for me to find out. 7 Q. Does it mean that your experiments in Belgrade depend on the assumption that those foils were people from the former Yugoslavia? 10 A. Yes. 11 Q. And, if not, that this test in Belgrade does not add anything to your test with Dutch subjects? 13 A. You have invited a scientist. It is more complicated, but the question is not are they from the former Yugoslavian Republic or not but how many. If one is not I would say there is still no problem. If only one is a former Yugoslavian then there is a problem. So it is matter of degree. But I would say it would be very nice to be assured that they all came from the former Republic of Yugoslavia. 20 Q. Actually did you show all 13 pictures to the subjects in Belgrade or a lesser amount of pictures? 22 A. No, we asked them to classify the 12, not the picture of Mr. Tadic, because we assumed that by now they would recognise this picture immediately and know that he is from the former Serbia. So that would be a meaningless question. We also did not want to suggest to them that what they were doing would contribute to this trial, because that could give them all sorts of second thoughts, second reasons, to answer to our questions instead of simply doing the task, which is classifying according to ethnic background. So we did not show that picture. It would not teach us anything that would be useful, and it would sort of threaten the neutrality of the test. 5 Q. By now what do you mean, when would it be no longer appropriate to run the test when the trial started or at an earlier date? 7 A. I think it would be very nice before the photospread was shown to anyone at all to test it thoroughly to see that it is not biased, to see that naive subjects from the group who was going to be interviewed later, people from Bosnia, that they would find it impossible, not having met Mr. Tadic before, to identify who the accused in that lineup is. That would be very nice. It would be a very wise precaution. Rule 1: Can an involvement in a crime be proved by means of a lineup or a show up when the suspect is known to the witness for other reasons than involvement in the crime? 10 A. I think we have discussed this before. Such a test would not logically place the witness at the scene of the crime. 12 Q. Thank you. Should identification of a suspect not known to the witness for other reasons than encounter during the crime be achieved by means of a lineup and not a show up? 15 A. Yes, by a "show up" in this rule I mean a one person test, and a one person test is not a difficult test to pass and it does not show that you really recognise this person; you only have to say "yes". 19 Q. Did you find any one person test in this case? 20 A. Well, not with the four witnesses that I would think are really relevant as identification subjects. They were all multi-person tests. 23 Q. Is the selection of a suspect through mug file inspection acceptable as proof of identify? 4 A. "Mug file inspections" usually mean a collection of pictures that are shown to a victim of a crime in order to find a suspect, not to recognise a suspect, but to first find during the investigation, say, the identity of a possible suspect. Those mug files are not selected on the basis of, say, the description or a detailed description and, therefore, cannot pass as a fair lineup or identity parade. Therefore, mug file inspections can be used for investigations, not as proof of identity. They are two different things. 13 Q. Have you found any mug file inspection in this case? 14 A. No, no. There is one problem, though, that, as I mentioned before, in a real identity parade, either, say, live or photographic, you would completely know who the foils are and that they are innocent, and we do not that right now. So there is a slight problem that, say, the nature of the spread that was used cannot be defined exactly, but I would not qualify it as just a simple mug file inspection because clearly it is not. It is better than that. 22 Q. Thank you. I jump to rule 7 now. Should the witness be asked to identify the same suspect more than once? 24 A. No, because if you show, say, the same suspect twice, that is suggestive. 26 Q. If I may jump to Rule 10 then, when there are more witnesses available, should a falsification of an initial identification be attempted? 1 A. Yes, in principle, when you have many witnesses, it is a good procedure to ask them all to identify the accused person. The reason is that is related to what we discussed before. You should, of course, never hide negative outcomes of identification tests, but you should also make -- give yourself the opportunity to get negative results. For instance -- but I must apologise because scientists always make these hypothetical cases and create problems thereby -- imagine that there are 10 witnesses and they just guess. One of them guesses correct. That might be the first one. If you now stop, you do not ask the other ones, you will never know that it was a guess. You have to ask them, all 10, and then you will find out that the others do not recognise them. So in order -- we would say you must -- you make yourself vulnerable after initial successes and be sure that it was not just a guess. That is why you should ask all witnesses to identify if they have seen the accused or if they have seen, no, the perpetrator. Right? If they have not seen anything that is relevant, they cannot make an identification. But if, in principle, they would be good identification witnesses, you should also use them. 23 Q. Thank you. If I may proceed to rule 11 then: Should all identification attempts, whether successful or not, be reported? 25 A. Yes. I think we have discussed that and the reason why is quite clear. 27 Q. Right. Would this include also witnesses who have not been called to testify in Court but who were interviewed during discovery, that is, pretrial stage but not called in Court? 2 A. Yes, in principle, I think every test that has been applied during the investigation process ought to be reported and made known to the Court, because if you do not do that, and of course I do not want to suspect anybody of bad intentions, but it would be possible, in principle, to hide the negative ones and propose the positives ones. 8 Q. If I proceed to rule 12 then: Should reports about identification attempts with negative results provide all available information that could help to understand the value? 11 A. Yes, very clearly, and a negative result may be completely uninteresting if we know that, in fact, the witness was an onlooker from 300 metres distance. Of course, that would be very difficult to identify. It does not mean the accused is not the wanted person. If the witness, on the contrary, was at a distance of one and a half metres and has watched on for several hours and he would be unable to identify the accused, that is highly informative because that suggests that possibly the accused is the wrong person. So you would want -- even the negative outcomes can highly informative, and can only be interpreted if you know, say, the conditions in which they occurred. 23 Q. Did the procedure that was applied to the witness we just discussed, that lady witness we just discussed, meet this rule? 25 A. It is very difficult for me to say that because, as you realise, I only received a limited number of pages relating to her testimony. So I am not completely sure about how much about that case is known to the Court. 1 Q. The Court has seen the same pages and heard the same evidence. 2 A. Yes, but I have not seen her complete testimony, I think, so I do not want to express opinions or judgments about things that maybe are different when I would have looked at the complete transcript of her testimony here in Court. 6 Q. I appreciate that. 7 A. If I now may proceed to rule 13: Will the probative value of an initial identification be increased through identification by other eyewitnesses, the number of the identifications? 16 A. Yes. The general idea of that rule is that, say, there is no linear relationship between the number of witnesses who identify and the amount of, say, trust that the Court should have. 19 Q. What does that mean? 20 A. Let me give you an example: if an accused has a twin brother who looks exactly like him, then it is quite possible that the first witness will be mistaken there and also quite likely that all the others will be mistaken in the same way. So you cannot then say, "Ah, but because now we have 20 witnesses it cannot be the twin brother". So, the sheer number of witnesses is not, say, the most relevant piece of information. For that reason, I would say, if I may refer to the present case, four witnesses, although compared to the 50, the 48 others may look a small number, in view of this rule, it would not be so extremely useful to find more than four who identify. If the procedure is correct and you can trust those identifications, I would say that is quite enough. Do not go for also another 48 or so. 6 Q. Thank you. If I proceed to rule 14: Should investigators do everything within their power to prevent contacts among witnesses? 9 A. Yes, yes, and on purpose this is formulated in this way to do everything within your power because it is not -- usually not within our power to prevent all contacts among witnesses. If they are father and son or wife and husband, then that simply cannot be avoided, especially not when the time between the crime and the appearance in Court is very long. Then, of course, it may happen that witnesses exchange information about the identity of possible perpetrators. But I think investigators should not aggravate that problem by adding, say, their own contacts when it can be avoided. There are a number of examples in cases where the investigation itself is the reason why witnesses came into contact with one another and that, I think, should be avoided. 22 Q. Would it be relevant then that more than one member of the same family is asked to participate in the photospread test? 24 A. Well, indeed, if it were possible to find witnesses who have not been in contact with one another, that would be much better than to get all witnesses from the same family. So if you want to choose four, it would be better to choose four totally independent ones than family members. If it is established that 1 they are family members and have been in contact, say, during a 2 long period and have discussed the case and identity of 3 perpetrators and so on, then of course it is quite possible, 4 generally speaking, that information about, say, the appearance 5 of a perpetrator is transferred from one person to the other. 6 Things about, well, the name itself might be highly suggestive 7 because if one did not recognise someone but the other did and 8 the first witness says, "Well, did you not recognise so and so?" 9 that may stick, of course, and the image then may be formed and 10 then the later recognition might follow. The beauty, of course, of, say, the multiple person 12 identity parade is that if the parade is organised well, it 13 would be very difficult to transfer information that would help 14 you to get at the correct choice. It will especially help you 15 if the parade is not well organised. So that, for instance, if 16 you say, "Well, he had dark hair", and there is only one with 17 dark hair in the spread, then such information might help. In a 18 good spread they would all have dark hair and it would not have 19 helped. So that is something that maybe is important to 20 notice. Some violations are not so bad in an isolated 22 situation. They may become terribly bad in combination with one 23 another. So this one, contacts among witnesses, and a not so 24 well chosen set of pictures in combination may make it suddenly 25 extremely easy for witnesses who do not remember the appearance 26 of the perpetrator to get at the right picture.

One can ask the witness to describe that image. It might be more or less vague, but the witness must be able to describe what it is. Is that an image of a man or of a woman? utterances.text: If I proceed to rule 19, Professor: Should the witness be instructed to identify only one person, that is the person he described, prior to the test? 3 A. Yes, in principle, the situation is if there are a number of people in front of you, if you recognise, say, the person you are asked to identify, there can be only one of them, and you cannot fire twice because that simply doubles the likelihood that you will have a hit. So you should indicate either none or one. 9 Q. That should be told to the ---- 10 A. And that should be told to the witness because it happens sometimes that witnesses are so quick that before you know it they have named two persons, and then what should you do? 13 Q. I take it, according to rule 20, that those instructions should be recorded? 15 A. Yes, in order to be certain that the proper instructions were given, it would be very nice to simply have them in the record. 17 Q. Dealing with these reports, does rule 20 have anything to do with the matter of certainty, for example, if different investigators run tests? 20 A. Yes, well, there is always the problem if you are afterwards asking an investigator whether there is one or many, how did you do it, you rely on their memory. I would say it is bad enough that you have to rely on the memory of witnesses, but that cannot be avoided. You should not complicate that by also having to rely on the memory of investigators which can be avoided. Now, the problem is, of course, if you have many investigators, if they have not agreed about a certain procedure, then the likelihood increases that they will have you different procedures, in fact, but the question is whether you will ever find out if they have not made a record of that. 4 Q. It is a problem, is it not? 5 A. It should not be a problem. 6 Q. If I may proceed to rule 21? Should the instruction to the witness stress that the wanted person is possibly not in the parade or in the photospread and that, therefore, a positive response should be made only when the witness is certain of recognising that person? 11 A. Yes, it is highly important that you tell the witness not to make an identification if the witness is not certain, because it is quite possible that there is no one here she can recognise. The research on, say, the presence or absence in instruction of that piece, in fact, is reported in the chapter that precedes this chapter, and that shows that it has, I would call it, a very large effect on the false positives on the identification of foils. 19 JUDGE STEPHEN: Could I just request the question? I see the word "mug shot" is used here again. What is your definition of a "mug shot" as distinct from a simple photograph? 22 A. Usually, mug shots or a mug shot collection is used as simply a number of photos from the police files, often with numbers on them but not necessarily, and there can be a large number. I say the largest number that I have seen being used was over 500. These mug shots are usually selected on the basis of a very, very superficial description of a perpetrator, and are selected in order to find the identity of a suspect. So, you do not have a suspect yet, there is no one you suspect but you try to find the identity of a suspect; whereas a photospread is constructed after you have a suspect because the suspect is one of them and the others (and usually not 500 but five to 10, say, would be quite enough) are selected especially in such a way that they resemble this one suspect. 7 Q. So that a mug shot is not a characteristic of a particular photograph, but rather of the time and ---- 9 A. Right. 10 Q. --- make up of the collection? 11 A. It is possible that, say, one picture appears in a mug shot and another time it appears in a proper photospread, but then it has been selected for that particular purpose. 14 JUDGE STEPHEN: Thank you. 15 MR. WLADIMIROFF: Looking to rule 22, Professor, I think you have answered or you have responded to that rule, that is, should police officers in charge of identification procedures have received the appropriate training and should they be able to demonstrate their professional qualifications both in written and oral testimony? 21 A. Yes, and the reason is that the procedures are, in fact, so much more difficult than you would think it is that you need training to do it, to do it right. 24 Q. If I may proceed to rule 28? Should all foils of an identity test fit the prior description obtained from witnesses? 26 A. Yes, if it does not, if they do not, then those foils might be easily discarded by the witness which makes the probability of just guessing who the accused is higher. 1 Q. If I may proceed to Rule 29? Can prior descriptions of the criminal that do not fit the suspect's appearance be used on the selection of foils? I think you answered to that rule too, did you not? 5 A. Yes, but I think that must be qualified because the question is, of course, what discrepancies are acceptable and what are not. What is really meant by rule 29 is that gross discrepancies, say, calling a man a woman or calling a white person a Japanese person or calling a very tall person a small person. That would qualify for some sort of dismissal of the situation. What does not qualify, for instance, is the absence or presence of a moustache, a beard, or things like that because they are considered to be minor things. Also, matters of length, age, weight, should be accepted with very wide margins because these things are not easily to perceive. 16 Q. As a matter of fact, you did address that matter in your letter of 10th October, Exhibit 91, that is, your letter to the Defence. You also gave an opinion on the problem of facial hair. Could you tell the Court what is the relevance of that problem or is this a relevancy at all? 21 A. Well, I took the freedom to comment on that because I saw it discussed so many times in the records and I thought, since apparently it is a problem to others, I should say something about it. The situation appears to be, as I understood it, that sometimes Mr. Tadic had facial hair growth and sometimes he had not. He was completely clean shaven or had a full beard and sometimes also he was badly shaven. Now, I would say to those who have known him for a 1 long time that would be no obstacle at all to recognise him in 2 any condition because they have seen him in all conditions. You 3 might in a way say they have in their memory they have pictures 4 of him in all various conditions and, no matter what he looks 5 like now, they would always be able to recognise him. For those who did not know him, the question is a 7 little bit more complicated, because if they have seen a person 8 committing a crime who was, say, clean shaven, just to give an 9 example, now they see an accused who has a full beard, you 10 would, in principle, be asking them to see through the beard 11 and, sort of, guess what this person would look like, say, 12 without the beard. Sometimes it was suggested that for that 13 reason accused people shave off their beards or let their beards 14 grow. But I would say the beauty of a well organised 16 identity test is that it solves that problem. If, say, the 17 picture shown to them has the wrong facial hair growth and they 18 can still recognise him, they recognise him, and it cannot be 19 guessing because the set up is so that guessing would not help 20 them. If they cannot recognise them, they do not recognise 21 them, period, then you have to ask, why do they not recognise 22 them? One of the explanations could be it is the hair growth. 23 But if they recognise them, then obviously the hair growth did 24 not pose a problem. So, logically, I would say for the large group of 26 witnesses who knew him hair growth can hardly be of any 27 relevance, and for those who did not know him, these four, well, 28 we had to test to see whether it posed a problem and, as much as we can trust the test, the result is it did not pose a problem. That is the beauty of such a test. 3 Q. If well performed? 4 A. If well performed, of course, yes. 5 Q. Talking about recognition and facial hair, what would be an appropriate distance for a live recognition in daytime? 7 A. Yes, I have published on that, I am not sure -- no, that is not in the list of literature I offered to you at the end of the letter of 10th October. I have a rather extensive publication on problems of distance and lighting conditions with respect to the recognition of faces, where it says that in daylight at a distance of more than 15 metres problems start. If there is a possibility that, say, two people look, are a bit similar, then from a distance of 15 metres the general, average observers start to make mistakes. I am not saying that at 15 metres you cannot recognise a person, but that is about where problems start, 15 metres. Less than 15 metres, I would say there is no problem. You would see whether that is the one individual that you know or not. Beyond 15 metres, that is the shortest distance at which problems start, and then, of course, the problems increase the longer the distance. 22 Q. Within 15 metres would facial hair be a problem? 23 A. No, not -- it depends again. We have to distinguish between these two groups. The group who knew him already before with facial hair might not have had a problem because that is the face they were used to. Those who did not know him and saw him for the first time there and then with the beard, initially there is no problem. They do not recognise anything at that time because that is their first perception of that person. Only later there is a problem, there might be a problem, because if the test presents someone without the facial hair, then they may not recognise him, but again the test solves that problem. That is the beauty of it. If the perception was not good enough initially, they will not recognise him, they will fail the test, and then we know it. If they recognised him in the test, apparently the perception was good enough. That is what the test proves. 10 Q. So if the basis is all right, that is, within 15 metres ---- 11 A. 15. 12 Q. --- if the basis is all right, then the story is valid as has been discussed today running a proper test? 14 A. Oh, no, maybe I have to correct you there. Even if they saw the perpetrator at a longer distance, it is quite possible that they saw him correctly and accurately, we can know that from the later test. That is what the test is for. If they did not perceive him correctly, they will fail the later test. The test is to show that their original perception was accurate enough, and in this situation you are now in, provided there are no doubts about the quality of the test, those four tests show that there were not these perception problems. But you have to be certain that there is no problem in the test. But if there is no problem, the beauty of the design of the test is that now you can be certain the perception was accurate. 26 MR. Mr. Kay seems to imply there that the investigator already knows that she did not say something, although she knew, and my question is how did the investigator know that? 12 Q. Let us see if we can address that question then. Let me ask you first about forms of recognition, because I noted in particular that you said that this witness did not express any recognition, did not recognise and so on. 16 A. No, I did not say that I think. She did not express it and then the rule is you should count her as someone who did not identify. 18 Q. Well, I think one of the quotes you had was "could not recognise" but let us not quibble about that. One of the forms of recognition, or one of the expressions of recognition, can be of course the simple statement, "I recognise that person as the one who did such and such", correct? 23 A. Right. 24 Q. It is also true to say that not all expressions of recognition need to be verbal. For example, someone can point in response to a question and that is also an indication of recognition. I take it would also be true that there are some reactions which are as demonstrative of recognition as pointing or speaking. For example, if someone encountered someone from whom they had great reason to fear and reacted by running from the room screaming in tears, that certainly might also be an expression of recognition, correct? 5 A. Well, now you come on very difficult ground, because if you accept all sorts of emotional, expression of emotions as recognition, then you are going to ask the investigator to interpret the behaviour of the witness. There you are on very slippery ground. Therefore, the procedure asks that the witness just says, "I indicated a number, that is the one I recognise." Points, indicates, says and no other less clear things because you would become dependent on all sorts of subjective interpretations of the investigator and you do not want that. 14 Q. Doctor, I appreciate you cannot ask a witness in lieu of verbal expression to have some physical reaction to the photograph or the individual to express their recognition. Of course that would not be practical. Nevertheless, that might happen, right? 18 A. Anything might happen. So what you would expect in that case is the investigator just describes what happens. 20 Q. Right, and in that case it might not be the investigator who is interpreting what is happening. It is the investigator bringing information to the court and allowing the Court to determine what happened? 24 A. If everything is described you can leave it to the Court to interpret it, yes, right. 26 Q. You would also agree, I take it, that that can be a very persuasive expression of one's recognition, a very sincere expression of one's recognition? 1 A. What can be a very sincere expression? 2 Q. An involuntary physical reaction. 3 A. Running from the room and screaming? 4 Q. Breaking out into a sweat, whatever kinds of physical expressions might result. 6 A. I would say breaking out into a sweat is exactly the thing I would have doubts about, because that is not easy to see, not always to easy to see and it is not always easy to attribute it just to recognition. It can be related to almost anything. So, no, I think when I say that there ought to be strict and clear procedures, some of the procedures relate to how the recognition is expressed. Some of the expressions are perfectly acceptable and clear and do not need to be quibbled with. Another thing, because they are doubtful and subject to personal interpretation which cannot be redone or undone by the Court because the Court cannot verify whether the investigator saw a sweat, I would say that is a less desirable procedure. I think to such a situation you ought to apply one of the rules that was formulated, which is if you can justify why by necessity you had to do it this way, I could not follow, say, the optimum procedure, maybe the Court should accept that. But if it cannot be justified, then I would not encourage investigators to do it that way. 23 Q. Doctor, the question was not intended to be, and I apologise if it seemed to be, a question which asked you to comment on the best possible procedure under those circumstances. I simply wanted to know whether you acknowledge that a recognition could be expressed in a variety of ways including a physical reaction? I think you agree with that, is that not true? 1 A. Oh, I think witnesses can do that. I do not want to have said that that should be acceptable as a procedure. 3 Q. Not as a procedure. You should focus on the existence of a recognition or not. 5 A. Rather you should instruct witnesses not to express it in other ways than by saying it and pointing at the right picture. 7 Q. Yes, I think I understood that from your earlier testimony as well. Let me ask you one more question. Is it also possible, in your view, that an individual who sees a photograph or a person who elicits great fear reacts to that fear by trying to distance himself or herself from the situation and verbally expressing or denying that recognition? 13 A. Yes, sure, I think that is perfectly possible. I do not think such a person makes a great witness. 15 Q. You read the full transcript of Mrs. Jaskic, is that right? 16 A. No. 17 Q. I am sorry, you read the pages you were given that included page 2977? 19 A. Would it be helpful if I tell you which pages I have? 20 Q. I actually have a list of that I believe so I can accompany you with that. 22 A. I had 53, 2953, 54, 55, then jumping to 62, then 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69 and that is the end. I do not know which proportion of the whole testimony that is. 25 Q. On page 2977 ---- 26 A. 2977, I did not have that one. 27 Q. You were not provided with that? 28 A. Oh, yes. Sure, OK, that is the next testimony. Right. That is by Mr. Paepen I think. 2 Q. That is right. The reaction that Mrs. Jaskic had at the time she viewed the photospread was described? 4 A. I think you have refer to me to the line. 5 Q. Doctor, I am referring to lines 27 through 32. 6 A. Yes. 7 Q. It seems you did not recall that? 8 A. Sure. No, I recall that. I do not know exactly what it means. 9 Q. Right, you do not know what it means? 10 A. No. 11 Q. This witness brought that to the Court? 12 A. Yes, sure but I do not know whether ---- 13 Q. It is for the Court to determine exactly what that means, is that not right? 15 A. No, if your suggestion is that one can conclude from that piece that obviously she recognised, I cannot conclude that. I can only see that she behaved in this way and then said "Go on". If you just stick to the rules it would say, so, that is not a recognition because then she should have said "That's him" and maybe run screaming from the room, but "Go on" sort of means that she would want to have a look at the other pictures. 22 Q. So it is not a recognition under the rules? 23 A. Under proper rules I would say do not count that as recognition. It is risky. You do not know exactly what happens, why she made that. If I may add, it is quite probably -- no, not probably. I should correct it. It is possible that the uncertainty of the situation has led to this. If her task was to recognise the one person she had mentioned, 1 I do not know whether she had mentioned the name Tadic, I think 2 she did, if she had been asked, "Well, that one person, is he in 3 this file or not?" and she recognised him, she might have said 4 here, "That's him, stop". If she was under the allusion that 5 she might see more people whom she had met in the camp, it could 6 it could have been possible for her to say after recognising 7 one, "Go on" expecting some more, you see. The unclarity or 8 maybe the possible impropriety of the procedure may have led to 9 this difficulty. I would say good procedures avoid also 10 interpretation problems. So, I do not even know what the "Go 11 on" means. Does she mean, "I am not sure whether it is him. Go 12 on, maybe we get a better picture of him". Or does she mean, 13 "Go on, maybe there are other criminals that I might also 14 recognise." It is sort of very difficult to interpret what this 15 all means and proper procedures avoid such difficulties.
